title: Kindness beyond

cards: A broken barrel of wine, and a court case. The Talmud, in tractate Bava Metzia, tells it. Porters carrying wine for a man named Rabbah bar bar Hanan break a barrel, so he takes their cloaks to cover the loss.
They go to Rav, the judge, and Rav tells him: give them back their cloaks. Rabbah asks the obvious question. Is that the law?
The porters did break his barrel. Rav's answer, and what he says next, hold today's word.

teach.h: INSIDE THE LINE OF THE LAW.
teach.b: Chesed. Loving-kindness, and here, kindness beyond what's owed. You met it long ago at the well, when Rebekah watered the camels too.
Turn it four ways. First, Rav's answer. Yes, he says, quoting Proverbs in the old Jewish translation: "That thou mayest walk in the way of good men."
The cloaks go back. Then the porters speak again: we're poor, we worked all day, we're hungry, and we have nothing. Pay them their wages, says Rav.
Is that the law? Yes, and he finishes the verse: "and keep the paths of the righteous."
The tradition's phrase for this is lifnim mishurat hadin, inside the line of the law: not breaking the law, but stepping back from what you're entitled to. Second, it's larger than charity.

teach.h: GREATER THAN CHARITY IN THREE WAYS.
teach.b: The Talmud, in tractate Sukkah, says loving-kindness is greater in three ways. Charity is given with money; kindness with your body too. Charity goes to the poor; kindness to poor and rich alike.
Charity is for the living; kindness reaches the living and the dead. Third, the world leans on it.
Simon the Just says, in Pirkei Avot, that the world stands on Torah, on worship, and on acts of loving-kindness.
Fourth, it doesn't keep a bill. Owed kindness keeps accounts. Chesed goes past them.
The verse of Micah that asks a person to walk humbly, back on humility day, also asks "to love mercy," and the Hebrew word there is chesed. Not to tolerate it. To love it.
Generosity opened the hand; chesed keeps it open after the bill is paid.

how: Jewish communities organize acts of loving-kindness, gemilut chasadim, such as free loan societies, meals for mourners and new parents, and visits to the sick, and Mussar students practice chesed by going one step past what's required.

o: pity felt for someone who is suffering
loving-kindness that gives past what's owed
charity given in money to the poor

p: inside the line of the law
the world stands on three things

s: going beyond what's owed means breaking the law to be kind
lifnim mishurat hadin means staying inside the law and stepping back from what you're entitled to.
the Talmud says loving-kindness is greater than charity in three ways
body as well as money, rich as well as poor, the dead as well as the living.
in Rav's case, the porters had to pay for the broken barrel
Rav told Rabbah to return their cloaks and pay their wages.

games.q: you're Rav. porters broke a barrel of wine, and the owner kept their cloaks. they say they're poor and hungry. what do you rule?
o: they owe for the wine; he keeps the cloaks.
return the cloaks, and pay them their wages.
split the loss down the middle.
games.why: Rav rules both, quoting Proverbs a half-verse at a time: "That thou mayest walk in the way of good men, and keep the paths of the righteous."

practice: Think of one place where you're owed something, or where you only give the minimum: a neighbor, a coworker, someone whose mistake cost you.

Look one step past the line, waving off a small debt, staying five more minutes, thanking someone who was only doing their job, and see that moment clearly. If you pray, you can carry that person into your prayer.

wordCard.voice: Chesed. Loving-kindness: giving past what's owed, with your body and your time as well as your money, to anyone at all. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: beyond what's owed. Chesed gives past the bill and doesn't keep one. Rest well tonight.

sources.q: That thou mayest walk in the way of good men, and keep the paths of the righteous.
